parties:
Proddut Kumar Das ------- Appellant
Vs.
A Rashid Howlader and others --------- Respondents
full_judgment: 17. The disputed land is presently situated at Amtali Upazila of Borguna District which was formerly included in the subdivision of Patuakhali. Defendant No.1 in support of his title to the suit land produced an unregistered salami receipt dated 5 Baishakh, 1359. BS and Dakhila dated 15.08.1360 BS. The trial Court and the Appellate Court were of the view that at date of execution of the salami receipts on 5 Baishakh, 1359 BS corresponding to 18th April 1952 AD Zamindari system was not prevalent because of the coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the SAT Act) and, therefore, Zamindars had no right to give pattan of their land at that time. But the High Court Division took a different view on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act stating that Part-V of this Act came into force in the Sub-Division of Patuakhali on 5th August, 1954 AD. The view taken by the High Court Division on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act appears to be correct since Part-V of the SAT Act came into force in entire area of Patuakhali Sub-Division of the District of Bakcrganj with effect from the date of publication of the notification in the Dacca Gazette, vide Notification No.9918-LR., date 8th July 1954, published in the Decca Gazette, date 5th August, 1954, Part-I, p. 890 (SAT ACT DLR by Obaidul Huq Chowdhury, Fifth Edition-2015, page 242- 243].Hence, in the Subdivision of Patuakhali Zamindars had right to give pattan of their land by receiving salami before 5th August, 1954. But the question pertaining to this case is whether Naeb Shailendra Nath Saha executing the salami receipt on behalf of the Zamindars gave the same to the father of defendant No.1, Tazem Ali Hawlader and delivered possession of the suit land to him or not? The salami receipts and rent receipts were marked as exhibits with objection. Salami receipt and dakhila are private documents and those will not be admissible in evidence as genuine documents on the mere production of the same. The genuineness of the salami receipt has to be determined in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. The Appellate Court held that the salami receipt/lease document is not genuine itself since it is rubbed and has cut marks and the back page of it is covered by white paper. This view of the Appellate Court regarding the title document of defendant No.1 seems to be based on proper appreciation of the documentary evidence on record in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In the case of Ajufannessa @ AjiBibi and others-Vs-Safar Miah and others, 30 D.L.R (AD) 41 it was held that "A private document can-not be taken notice of and marked as an Exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may, however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a person, as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a landlord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. In this case, both of the courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or procedure which had affected the merits of the case." The ratio of this case was again reiterated in the case of Md. Jashimuddins Kanchan -Vs- Md. Ali Ashraf (42 DLR (AD) 289]. The High Court Division did not reverse this finding of the Appellate Court that the genuineness of the salami receipt is highly doubtful. Since the tide document of the father of defendant No.1 is highly doubtful, subsequent transfer of the same property to defendant No.1 by oral gift is also doubtful. Defendant No.1 claimed that during 1961 his house at the disputed land was destroyed by cyclone for which he repaired the same with his own expense. But he deposed,  “১৯৬১ সালে আমি ৬ষ্ঠ শ্রেণীতে পড়তাম। তখন আমার ব্যক্তিগত আয়ের উৎস ছিলনা।" This portion of the deposition of Dv-1 suggests that the claim of defendant No.1 regarding his possession of the suit property from 1960 onward is apparently baseless. It appears that father of defendant No.1 and thereafter, defendant No.1 did not take any time worthy step whatsoever for correction of the record of rights. The possession of the defendant No.1 in the suit land cannot be traced back to any valid title whereas the possession (before dispossession) of the plaintiffs in the suit land can be traced back to valid title which coupled with attending facts and circumstances reasonably gives rise to the presumption that the plaintiffs were dispossessed from the suit land by defendant No.1 by force.
